about: Search guide for BibleChat (phone and computer). Hand-written and checked by tests/test_guide.py: every reference exists, every Hebrew/Greek note names a Strong's number that stands in that verse, and every topic linked to a Study Path has each of its themes inside the path. It holds references and short notes only, never verse text. Notes are BibleChat's, not Scripture, and the app labels them so.

deutero.long: This book is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, but not in Protestant ones (the King James printed it among the Apocrypha).

orthodox.long: This book is in Orthodox Bibles, but not in Catholic or Protestant ones.

orthodox_appendix.long: This book is printed in an appendix of Greek Orthodox Bibles. It is not in Catholic or Protestant Bibles.

esdras2.long: This book (also called 4 Ezra) is in the Ethiopian and Slavonic Bibles and the King James Apocrypha, but not in the Catholic or Protestant canon.

ethiopian.long: This book is in the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church only. Other churches do not count it as Scripture.

noncanon.long: This is an old writing that no church counts as Scripture today. BibleChat includes it with the Ethiopian Canon so it can be read and compared.

letter.long: 1 Clement is a letter from the church at Rome to Corinth (about AD 96). It is not in today's Bibles; one old Greek Bible, Codex Alexandrinus, copied it after Revelation.

jasher.long: The 1840 English Book of Jasher. Scholars dispute whether it is the book named in Joshua 10:13 and 2 Samuel 1:18. No church counts it as Scripture.

original.text: "Those that published it" is one Hebrew word, a feminine plural form of basar, "to bring good news". The Hebrew says the ones who proclaim are women, so many translations read "the women who proclaim it are a great host". The King James "those" does not show it.

"That bringest good tidings" is a feminine form of basar, "to bring good news": Zion and Jerusalem are pictured as a woman who carries the news. Some translations read "O Zion, herald of good tidings"; others "you who bring good tidings to Zion".
"Man" here is the Hebrew 'adam, "a human being" or "mankind". The same verse explains it: "male" (zakar) "and female" (neqebah) created he them.

"Help meet" is two Hebrew words: 'ezer, "help", and kenegdo, "corresponding to him" or "his counterpart". The Bible also calls God our 'ezer: "My help cometh from the LORD" (Psalms 121:2), "he is our help and our shield" (Psalms 33:20).

"Desire" is teshuqah, a rare Hebrew word found only three times: here, in Genesis 4:7 (sin's desire for Cain, which he must rule over) and in Song of Solomon 7:10 ("his desire is toward me"). Readers differ on which sense fits this verse.

context.text: God speaks to the woman after the fall, between His words to the serpent and to Adam (3:14-19), where the ground is cursed and Adam will labour and return to dust. Before the fall both were told together to "have dominion" (1:28). Christians differ on whether "he shall rule over thee" is a command or a description of what sin brings.

original.text: Deborah is a nebiy'ah, "prophetess", the word also used for Miriam (Exodus 15:20) and Huldah (2 Kings 22:14), and she "judged Israel". "Lapidoth" means "torches"; most read it as her husband's name, a few as a description, "a woman of fire".
"Virtuous" is chayil, "strength, valour, ability, wealth". It is the same word as in "thou mighty man of valour" (Judges 6:12), and Boaz calls Ruth "a virtuous woman" with it (Ruth 3:11).

"Train up" is chanak, also used for dedicating a new house (Deuteronomy 20:5). "In the way he should go" is literally "according to his way"; readers take it as the right way, or as each child's own bent.
"Follow" is radaph, which usually means "pursue" or "chase" ("Let the enemy persecute my soul", Psalms 7:5). Goodness and mercy do not just come after; they run after.
"Be still" is raphah, "let go, slacken, cease". In this psalm about wars and nations (46:6-9) it is read as "stop striving" as much as "be quiet".

"Virgin" is the Hebrew 'almah, "a young woman" of age to marry. Matthew 1:23 quotes the verse with the Greek parthenos, "virgin", as the old Greek translation (the Septuagint) had it. Translations of Isaiah differ: "virgin" or "young woman".

The Hebrew of this line is hard and translations differ: "he hateth putting away" (King James), "I hate divorce", or "the man who hates and divorces his wife covers his garment with violence". All of them read it in the setting of verses 14-15, a man dealing "treacherously" with "the wife of thy youth".

"Little children" is na'arim qetannim. Na'ar is used for young men too: Abraham's "young men" (Genesis 22:3) and Joseph at seventeen (Genesis 37:2). Bethel was the centre of the golden calf worship (1 Kings 12:28-29), and the youths mocked the prophet on his way there.

"Peter" is Petros and "rock" is petra, two related Greek words for stone and rock. Christians read "this rock" as Peter himself, as Peter's confession that Jesus is "the Christ, the Son of the living God" (16:16), or as Christ.

Jesus asks twice with agapao ("lovest thou me?", verses 15-16) and the third time with phileo (verse 17); Peter answers each time with phileo. English has "love" for both. Readers differ on whether the change of word matters.
This third time Jesus uses Peter's own word, phileo, for "lovest thou me?" (verses 15-16 have agapao). Readers differ on whether the change of word matters.

"Servant" is diakonos, the word the King James translates "deacon" in 1 Timothy 3:8 and "minister" in Romans 13:4 and Ephesians 6:21. Phebe is a diakonos "of the church which is at Cenchrea". Translations differ: "servant", "deacon", "deaconess", "minister".

"Helpers" is synergos, "fellow worker", the word Paul uses for Timothy ("my workfellow", Romans 16:21) and Titus ("fellowhelper", 2 Corinthians 8:23). Priscilla is named first here, as in Acts 18:18 and 2 Timothy 4:19.

The Greek form can be the woman's name Junia, a common Roman name, or a man's name Junias, which is not found in any other ancient writing. The King James and early church writers such as John Chrysostom read a woman. "Of note among the apostles" is read as "outstanding among the apostles" or as "well known to the apostles".
"Laboured with me" is synathleo, "to strive together" like athletes, the word in "striving together for the faith of the gospel" (Philippians 1:27). "Those women" are Euodias and Syntyche of verse 2.
"Servants" and "handmaidens" are the male and female forms of one Greek word, doulos and doule. The Spirit is poured on both, and both "shall prophesy", as Joel 2:29 says.
"Ministered" is diakoneo, the verb of diakonos ("deacon", "minister"). The women supported Jesus and the twelve "of their substance", from their own means.
"Power" is exousia, "authority": the Greek says "to have authority on her head". Some translations add words ("a sign of authority"); others read it as authority over her own head.

The Greek gyne means both "woman" and "wife"; verse 35 ("let them ask their husbands at home") is why some translations read "wives". "Keep silence" is sigao, the same verb Paul uses in this chapter for a tongue-speaker with no interpreter (14:28) and a prophet when another receives a revelation (14:30).

context.text: Paul is writing to the church at Corinth about order in its meetings (14:26-40): "Let all things be done decently and in order." Earlier in the same letter women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5). Christians read these verses together in different ways: as a rule for all churches, as a word about disruptive questions in Corinth, or as a limit on judging prophecy.
Part of Paul's words on order in the meetings at Corinth (14:26-40). In the same letter women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5). Christians read these verses together in different ways.

original.text: "Usurp authority over" is authenteo, a Greek verb found only here in the Bible; its exact sense is debated ("to have authority", "to domineer"). "Silence" is hesuchia, "quietness", the word in "with quietness they work" (2 Thessalonians 3:12); a related word is in "a quiet and peaceable life" (1 Timothy 2:2).

context.text: Paul writes to Timothy, whom he left at Ephesus to stop false teachers (1:3-7; 4:1-7). He grounds these words in Genesis 2 and 3 (2:13-14). Christians differ on whether they are a rule for all churches and all teaching, or a word for the situation in Ephesus. In Acts, Priscilla and Aquila together taught Apollos "the way of God more perfectly" (Acts 18:26).

Paul gives the reason for verses 11-12 from Genesis 2 and 3. "She shall be saved in childbearing" is one of the hardest lines in the New Testament to translate; readers take it as the birth of Christ, as safety in childbirth, or as a woman's faithful life.

Paul writes to Corinth about how men and women pray and prophesy in worship, and asks the woman to cover her head. In the same passage he adds "neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord" (11:11-12). He appeals to creation, to nature and to the custom of "the churches of God" (11:16). Christians differ on whether the covering is a lasting rule or a custom of that time.

original.text: "Submit yourselves" is hupotasso, the same verb as in verse 21, "Submitting yourselves one to another". Some of the oldest Greek manuscripts have no verb in verse 22 and carry it over from verse 21.

context.text: Paul writes to the church at Ephesus. The verse before says "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God" (5:21); the verses after tell husbands "love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" (5:25-33). Christians differ on how verses 21 and 22 fit together.

Paul's household instructions to the church at Colossae, given in pairs: wives and husbands ("love your wives, and be not bitter against them"), children and fathers ("provoke not your children"), servants and masters (3:18-4:1).

Peter writes to Christians scattered in Asia Minor (1:1), many with unbelieving husbands or masters (2:18-3:2). He hopes husbands "may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives". Verse 7 turns to husbands: honour the wife, "heirs together of the grace of life".

original.text: "Heirs together" is one Greek word, synkleronomos, "co-heir". "Weaker" is asthenes, "without strength"; the verse joins it to honour, not to lesser worth.
"Male" and "female" are arsen and thelus, the words Jesus uses for creation: "made them male and female" (Matthew 19:4). The Greek here reads "there is no male and female", echoing Genesis 1:27.

context.text: Paul to Titus in Crete: the aged women are to be "teachers of good things" (2:3) to the young women. The reason given is "that the word of God be not blasphemed" (2:5); servants get a like reason, "that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour" (2:10).

Written by Jesus son of Sirach, a Jewish teacher in Jerusalem (about 180 BC), in a section on what a father worries about and must guard (42:9-14). Sirach is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but not in Protestant ones. The same book also says "Blessed is the man that hath a virtuous wife" (26:1).

A wisdom saying: a short observation about life, not a law. Proverbs also says "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing" (18:22), warns about the contentious man (26:21) and ends with the virtuous woman (31:10-31).
A wisdom saying, not a law. Proverbs also says "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing" (18:22) and warns about the contentious man (26:21).

The Preacher's search for "the reason of things" (7:25-29). He ends with words about all people: "God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions" (7:29). The same book says "Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest" (9:9).

The two oldest complete Greek manuscripts of Mark (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, 4th century) end at 16:8. Most later manuscripts, and the King James, have verses 9-20. Many modern Bibles print them with a note.
The woman taken in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) is not in the oldest Greek manuscripts of John. Many modern Bibles print it with a note or in brackets.

The words "in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one" are in the King James, but in no Greek manuscript before the late Middle Ages. Erasmus added them in his third edition (1522). Most modern Bibles leave them out or put them in a note.
This verse is not in the oldest Greek manuscripts of Acts; the King James follows later texts that have it. Many modern Bibles put it in a note.
Jesus says this to Pharisees who had just said He cast out devils by Beelzebub (12:22-24). Mark adds: "Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit" (Mark 3:30).

Written to Hebrew Christians tempted to turn back (10:32-39). Right after, the writer adds: "But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you" (6:9). Christians read the warning differently: about believers who fall away, or about people who tasted the gospel but never truly believed.

Jesus speaks to the great crowds about the cost of following Him (14:25-33). Matthew gives the same teaching as "He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10:37). Jesus also upheld "Honour thy father and mother" (Matthew 15:4).
Jesus sends out the twelve (10:5-42). The next verses explain the sword as division in families over Him (10:35-36), in words from Micah 7:6. Luke has "division" (Luke 12:51).

A lament of the exiles in Babylon (137:1-4), crying to God about what was done to Jerusalem (137:7-8). It records their anguish in prayer; it is not a command. Jesus teaches "Love your enemies" (Matthew 5:44).

Samuel gives Saul the LORD's judgment on Amalek for attacking Israel on the way out of Egypt (15:2; Exodus 17:8-16; Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Readers have long wrestled with this command. The Bible also says God has "no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezekiel 33:11).

The Bible presents this as judgment on the sins of the Canaanites (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4-5). Rahab and her family, who believed, were spared (6:25). Readers have long wrestled with these passages.

Paul writes to a church where many believers were slaves. The same passage tells masters to stop threatening, "knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him" (6:9). Paul tells a slave "if thou mayest be made free, use it rather" (1 Corinthians 7:21), and sends Onesimus back "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved" (Philemon 1:16).

Malachi speaks of two peoples, Israel (Jacob) and Edom (Esau) (1:4). Paul quotes it about God's choosing, "not of works, but of him that calleth" (Romans 9:11-13). "Hated" is often read as "loved less" or "not chosen", as when "Leah was hated" (Genesis 29:30-31).
Paul quotes Malachi 1:2-3, where Jacob and Esau stand for the peoples Israel and Edom. "Hated" is often read as "loved less" or "not chosen", as when "Leah was hated" (Genesis 29:30-31).

A wisdom saying about loving correction: "he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes". Proverbs pictures discipline as love (3:11-12, quoted in Hebrews 12:5-6). Paul adds "Fathers, provoke not your children to wrath" (Ephesians 6:4). Readers differ on whether "rod" means physical punishment or correction in general.

Jesus answers Pharisees who came "tempting him" (19:3). Matthew has "except it be for fornication" (also 5:32); Mark 10:11-12 and Luke 16:18 give no exception. Paul adds the case of an unbelieving spouse who departs (1 Corinthians 7:15). Christians differ on when divorce and remarriage are allowed.

Paul is answering a letter from Corinth ("the things whereof ye wrote unto me"). Many read "It is good for a man not to touch a woman" as a saying from that letter, which Paul then answers in verses 2-5; some translations put it in quotation marks. He also calls not marrying a gift (7:7).

James writes against a faith that does nothing (2:14-17); Paul, in Romans 3:28, writes against earning God's favour by "the deeds of the law". Both quote Genesis 15:6 about Abraham (James 2:23, Romans 4:3).
Paul writes against earning God's favour by "the deeds of the law"; James 2:24 writes against a faith that does nothing. Both quote Genesis 15:6 about Abraham (Romans 4:3, James 2:23).
Readers differ on "this generation": the people alive then (the temple fell in AD 70, as foretold in 24:1-2), the generation that sees these signs, or the Jewish people as a whole.

Christians read the thousand years in different ways: a future reign of Christ on earth after He returns (premillennial), the present age between His first and second coming (amillennial), or a time of the gospel's growth before He returns (postmillennial).

original.text: The Greek has no "the": "a root of all kinds of evil" (rhiza panton ton kakon). The warning is about the love of money (philarguria), not money itself.

context.text: God speaks to Judah after the exile, who were robbing Him "in tithes and offerings" (3:8-9); the tithe kept the Levites and the storehouse (Nehemiah 13:10-12). In the New Testament Paul teaches giving "as he purposeth in his heart; not grudgingly, or of necessity" (2 Corinthians 9:7). Christians differ on whether the tithe is required today.
The disciples were "astonished out of measure", and Jesus answered "with God all things are possible" (10:26-27). The story that a small "Needle Gate" in Jerusalem is meant has no early source.
Other verses say what asking "in my name" includes: "according to his will" (1 John 5:14), "If ye abide in me" (John 15:7), not asking "amiss" (James 4:3).

Jesus is speaking about lust (5:27-28) with strong pictures. Through history Christians have read this as a call to cut off what leads to sin, not as a command to harm the body; Paul calls the body "the temple of the Holy Ghost" (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Words shouted by a crowd in Jerusalem, reported by Matthew. This verse has been wrongly used to blame all Jews; Jesus prayed "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34), and Peter says the rulers acted "through ignorance" (Acts 3:17).

Paul writes to Thessalonians, some of whom had stopped working and were living "disorderly" (3:11). It is about those who will not work, not those who cannot; Paul also urges care for widows and the poor (1 Timothy 5:3, Galatians 2:10).
Paul writes to Christians in Rome under the emperor. When the rulers told the apostles to stop preaching, they answered "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29).

original.text: "Take no thought" is merimnao, "be anxious, worry", the same word as "Be careful for nothing" in Philippians 4:6. Jesus is not saying "don't plan" but "don't worry".
"Careful" is merimnao, "be anxious, worry", the word Jesus uses in "take no thought for the morrow" (Matthew 6:34). Modern Bibles read "Be anxious for nothing" or "Do not worry about anything".
"God" is Elohim, a plural form, with the singular verb bara, "created". The Bible uses bara only with God as the one who creates.
"Given by inspiration of God" is one Greek word, theopneustos, "God-breathed".
"Substance" is hupostasis, literally "a standing under": a foundation, an assurance. The same word is "confidence" in Hebrews 3:14.
"Workmanship" is poiema, "a thing made". It is used only twice in the New Testament: here and for God's creation in Romans 1:20 ("the things that are made").
"Caught up" is harpazo, "to seize, snatch". The Latin Bible translates it rapiemur, from which the English word "rapture" comes.
"Reasonable" is logikos, "of the mind, rational"; "service" is latreia, the word for worship in the temple (Romans 9:4). Modern Bibles read "spiritual worship" or "reasonable service".
